Eggs of the White-browed scimitar babbler, Pomatorhinus schisticeps, are incubated within domed nests woven from bamboo leaves and grass, a behavior common among the Timaliidae. Respirometry trials conducted on eggs at a stable temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] revealed that embryonic development culminates in hatching after precisely 19.5 days [ab = 19.5 days], a duration typical for passerines of moderate egg size within this thermoregulatory range. The relatively short incubation period likely reflects the benefits of sustained parental heat provisioning in tropical evergreen forests, where ambient thermal fluctuations are modest. Nestlings emerge at this point weighing approximately 3.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.6 grams], a wet weight at birth that is modest in absolute terms but consistent with the altricial developmental strategy observed across the babblers. This initial mass represents roughly eight percent of the eventual adult female mass, underscoring the substantial somatic growth that must occur during the nestling and fledgling phases.

At the active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] typically recorded in this species, the developmental trajectory of the nestling proceeds rapidly. Fledging, the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at approximately 16.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 16.5 days after hatching] under these thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This is a relatively brief nestling period for a bird of its adult body size, potentially an adaptation to reduce predation risk in dense understory habitats. The chick progresses through a predictable sequence of feather emergence and motor coordination, relying entirely on biparental provisioning throughout. After leaving the nest, the fledgling enters a post-fledging dependency phase during which it remains within the parental territory, gradually acquiring foraging skills such as probing leaf litter for invertebrates, before complete independence is achieved several weeks later.

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to produce viable gametes, is attained relatively early in the life cycle of this babbler. At the same body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] associated with active metabolism, the time since hatching to puberty is 37.5 days [tp = 37.5 days]. This rapid maturation is somewhat unusual for a bird that attains an ultimate wet weight for females of 43 grams [Wwi = 43 grams], as typical allometric scaling would predict a longer developmental period. The relatively early onset of gonad maturation may be facilitated by the consistently high resource availability in its Southeast Asian range, allowing individuals to allocate sufficient energy to structural growth and reproductive tissue development concurrently. Juveniles that achieve this milestone then enter a brief sub-adult phase before engaging in their first breeding cycle, which is influenced by both seasonal rainfall patterns and social competition for territories.

The initiation of first reproduction, rather than being coincident with puberty, is deferred until later in the life history of the Pomatorhinus schisticeps. Under the same standard body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the first successful breeding event occurs at 1.3 years since hatching [tR = 1.3 years since hatching]. This interval between reaching sexual maturity and actually producing offspring likely reflects the time required to establish a breeding territory and secure a mate, both of which are energetically demanding processes in year-round territorial species. Once breeding commences, females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], with clutch sizes varying between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 and 5 eggs per clutch]. This modest annual reproductive output is characteristic of tropical insectivores that invest substantially in prolonged parental care, resulting in high per-offspring survival at the expense of total fecundity.

Maximum longevity in this species, as determined from field-based mark-recapture studies conducted at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] under optimal thermal conditions, has been documented at 9.4 years [am = 9.4 years]. This lifespan, while modest compared to some larger rainforest passerines, aligns well with predictions based on the species' adult body mass of 43 grams in females and the typical survivorship curves of tropical Timaliidae. The relatively low annual reproductive output is thus offset by an extended reproductive window, with adults potentially breeding for eight or more years. Correspondingly, the basal metabolic rate measured in resting post-absorptive adults is 75.16 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 75.16 milliliters of oxygen per hour], supporting both the costs of thermoregulation in a humid environment and the sustained activity needed to forage for arthropod prey throughout the day at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
